:::: {.content-panel .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
::: {.sl-container .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
# Default Constructors {#_top .astro-np5lzwrf}
:::
::::

::::::: {.content-panel .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
:::::: {.sl-container .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
::::: sl-markdown-content
When working with data structures, it can be helpful to create values
that conform to a schema with minimal effort. For this purpose, the
Schema module provides default constructors for various schema types,
including `Structs`{dir="auto"}, `Records`{dir="auto"},
`filters`{dir="auto"}, and `brands`{dir="auto"}.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){.starlight-aside__icon
.astro-4rgy7crp} Constructor Scope

::: starlight-aside__content
Default constructors associated with a schema of type
`Schema<A, I, R>`{dir="auto"} operate specifically on the **decoded
type** (`A`{dir="auto"}), not the encoded type (`I`{dir="auto"}).

- **`A`{dir="auto"} (Decoded Type)**: This is the type produced after
  decoding and validation. The constructor creates values of this type.
- `I`{dir="auto"} (Encoded Type): This is the type expected when
  decoding raw input. The constructor does not accept this type
  directly.

This distinction is important when working with schemas that transform
data. For example, if a schema **decodes a string into a number**, the
default constructor will only accept **numbers**, not strings.
:::

Default constructors are **unsafe**, meaning they **throw an error** if
the input does not conform to the schema. If you need a safer
alternative, consider using
[Schema.validateEither](index.html#error-handling-in-constructors),
which returns a result indicating success or failure instead of throwing
an error.

**Example** (Using a Refinement Default Constructor)

::: twoslash-popup-docs
This schema transforms a `string` into a `number` by parsing the string
using the `parse` function of the `effect/Number` module.

It returns an error if the value can\'t be converted (for example when
non-numeric characters are provided).

The following special string values are supported: \"NaN\",
\"Infinity\", \"-Infinity\".
:::

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::
:::::

:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)
for more information.

## Structs

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#structs){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="structs"}
:::

Struct schemas allow you to define objects with specific fields and
constraints. The `make`{dir="auto"} function can be used to create
instances of a struct schema.

**Example** (Creating Struct Instances)

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame not-content">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>1import { import Schema</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

## Records

## Branded Types

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#branded-types){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="branded-types"}
:::

Branded schemas add metadata to a value to give it a more specific type,
while still retaining its original type.

When using default constructors, it is helpful to understand the type of
value they produce.

For instance, in the `BrandedNumberSchema`{dir="auto"} example, the
return type of the constructor is
`number & Brand<"MyNumber">`{dir="auto"}. This indicates that the
resulting value is a `number`{dir="auto"} with additional branding
information, `"MyNumber"`{dir="auto"}.

This behavior contrasts with the filter example, where the return type
is simply `number`{dir="auto"}. Branding adds an extra layer of type
information, which can assist in identifying and working with your data
more effectively.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## Error Handling in Constructors

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#error-handling-in-constructors){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="error-handling-in-constructors"}
:::

Default constructors are considered "unsafe" because they throw an error
if the input does not conform to the schema. This error includes a
detailed description of what went wrong. The intention behind default
constructors is to provide a straightforward way to create valid values,
such as for tests or configurations, where invalid inputs are expected
to be exceptional cases.

If you need a "safe" constructor that does not throw errors but instead
returns a result indicating success or failure, you can use
`Schema.validateEither`{dir="auto"}.

**Example** (Using `Schema.validateEither`{dir="auto"} for Safe
Validation)

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame not-content">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>1import { import Schema</code></pre>
</figure>

::: twoslash-popup-docs
This schema transforms a `string` into a `number` by parsing the string
using the `parse` function of the `effect/Number` module.

It returns an error if the value can\'t be converted (for example when
non-numeric characters are provided).

The following special string values are supported: \"NaN\",
\"Infinity\", \"-Infinity\".
:::

</figure>

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::
:::::

::: {.twoslash-popup-docs .twoslash-popup-docs-tags}
[\@see]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-name} ―
[[source](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v22.x/lib/console.js)]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-value}
:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)
for more information.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## Setting Default Values

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#setting-default-values){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="setting-default-values"}
:::

When creating objects, you might want to assign default values to
certain fields to simplify object construction. The
`Schema.withConstructorDefault`{dir="auto"} function lets you handle
default values, making fields optional in the default constructor.

**Example** (Struct with Required Fields)

In this example, all fields are required when creating a new instance.

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::
:::::

::: {.twoslash-popup-docs .twoslash-popup-docs-tags}
[\@see]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-name} ―
[[source](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v22.x/lib/console.js)]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-value}
:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)
for more information.
::::

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>var console: Console</code></pre>
</figure>

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::
:::::

::: {.twoslash-popup-docs .twoslash-popup-docs-tags}
[\@see]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-name} ―
[[source](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v22.x/lib/console.js)]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-value}
:::

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>Console.log(message?: any, ...optionalParams: any[]): void</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)
for more information.
::::

### Nested Structs and Shallow Defaults

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#nested-structs-and-shallow-defaults){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="nested-structs-and-shallow-defaults"}
:::

Default values in schemas are shallow, meaning that defaults defined in
nested structs do not automatically propagate to the top-level
constructor.

**Example** (Shallow Defaults in Nested Structs)

<figure class="frame not-content">

This behavior occurs because the `Schema`{dir="auto"} interface does not
include a type parameter to carry over default constructor types from
nested structs.

To work around this limitation, extract the constructor for the nested
struct and apply it to its fields directly. This ensures that the nested
defaults are respected.

**Example** (Using Nested Struct Constructors)

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame not-content">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>1import { import Schema</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

[Schema]{style="--0:#24292E;--1:#E1E4E8"}[ }
]{style="--0:#24292E;--1:#E1E4E8"}[from]{style="--0:#BF3441;--1:#F97583"}[
]{style="--0:#24292E;--1:#E1E4E8"}[\"effect\"]{style="--0:#032F62;--1:#9ECBFF"}

<pre data-language="ts"><code>var console: Console</code></pre>
</figure>

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::
:::::

::: {.twoslash-popup-docs .twoslash-popup-docs-tags}
[\@see]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-name} ―
[[source](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v22.x/lib/console.js)]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-value}
:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)
for more information.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h3 tabindex="-1"}
### Lazy Evaluation of Defaults

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#lazy-evaluation-of-defaults){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="lazy-evaluation-of-defaults"}
:::

Defaults are lazily evaluated, meaning that a new instance of the
default is generated every time the constructor is called:

**Example** (Lazy Evaluation of Defaults)

In this example, the `timestamp`{dir="auto"} field generates a new value
for each instance.

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

</figure>

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::
:::::

::: {.twoslash-popup-docs .twoslash-popup-docs-tags}
[\@see]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-name} ―
[[source](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v22.x/lib/console.js)]{.twoslash-popup-docs-tag-value}
:::
::::::::

[console]{style="--0:#24292E;--1:#E1E4E8"}[.]{style="--0:#24292E;--1:#E1E4E8"}[[]{.twoslash-hover}]{.twoslash
style="--0:#6F42C1;--1:#B392F0"}

::::::: {.twoslash-popup-container .not-content}
[]{.twoslash-popup-code-type}

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>Console.log(message?: any, ...optionalParams: any[]): void</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h3 tabindex="-1"}
### Using Defaults in Classes

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#using-defaults-in-classes){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="using-defaults-in-classes"}

Default values can also be applied when working with the
`Class`{dir="auto"} API, ensuring consistency across class-based
schemas.

::::: twoslash-popup-docs
The `console` module provides a simple debugging console that is similar
to the JavaScript console mechanism provided by web browsers.

The module exports two specific components:

- A `Console` class with methods such as `console.log()`,
  `console.error()` and `console.warn()` that can be used to write to
  any Node.js stream.
- A global `console` instance configured to write to
  [`process.stdout`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstdout)
  and
  [`process.stderr`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#processstderr).
  The global `console` can be used without importing the `node:console`
  module.

***Warning***: The global console object\'s methods are neither
consistently synchronous like the browser APIs they resemble, nor are
they consistently asynchronous like all other Node.js streams. See the
[`note on process I/O`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/process.html#a-note-on-process-io)
for more information.

Example using the global `console`:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>console.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to stdoutconsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints error message and stack trace to stderr://   Error: Whoops, something bad happened//     at [eval]:5:15//     at Script.runInThisContext (node:vm:132:18)//     at Object.runInThisContext (node:vm:309:38)//     at node:internal/process/execution:77:19//     at [eval]-wrapper:6:22//     at evalScript (node:internal/process/execution:76:60)//     at node:internal/main/eval_string:23:3
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;console.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to stderr</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

Example using the `Console` class:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const out = getStreamSomehow();const err = getStreamSomehow();const myConsole = new console.Console(out, err);
myConsole.log(&#39;hello world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.log(&#39;hello %s&#39;, &#39;world&#39;);// Prints: hello world, to outmyConsole.error(new Error(&#39;Whoops, something bad happened&#39;));// Prints: [Error: Whoops, something bad happened], to err
const name = &#39;Will Robinson&#39;;myConsole.warn(`Danger ${name}! Danger!`);// Prints: Danger Will Robinson! Danger!, to err</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

:::: twoslash-popup-docs
Prints to `stdout` with newline. Multiple arguments can be passed, with
the first used as the primary message and all additional used as
substitution values similar to
[`printf(3)`](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/printf.3.html) (the
arguments are all passed to
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)).

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame">
<pre data-language="js"><code>const count = 5;console.log(&#39;count: %d&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdoutconsole.log(&#39;count:&#39;, count);// Prints: count: 5, to stdout</code></pre>
</figure>
:::

See
[`util.format()`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args)
for more information.
